claim: E. faecium and its secreted peptidoglycan hydrolase (SagA) were sufficient to enhance intestinal barrier function and pathogen tolerance.
source: We discovered that Enterococcus faecium (E. faecium), a ubiquitous commensal bacterium, and its secreted peptidoglycan hydrolase (SagA) were sufficient to enhance intestinal barrier function and pathogen tolerance, but the precise biochemical mechanism was unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior experimental findings referenced in the abstract.

claim: E. faecium has unique peptidoglycan composition and remodeling activity through SagA.
source: Here we show E. faecium has unique peptidoglycan composition and remodeling activity through SagA, which generates smaller muropeptides that more effectively activates nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2) in mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing peptidoglycan analysis and NOD2 activation assays.

claim: SagA generates smaller muropeptides that more effectively activate NOD2 in mammalian cells.
source: Here we show E. faecium has unique peptidoglycan composition and remodeling activity through SagA, which generates smaller muropeptides that more effectively activates nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2) in mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing muropeptide generation and NOD2 activation assays.

claim: SagA is a NlpC/p60-endopeptidase that preferentially hydrolyzes crosslinked Lys-type peptidoglycan fragments.
source: Our structural and biochemical studies show that SagA is a NlpC/p60-endopeptidase that preferentially hydrolyzes crosslinked Lys-type peptidoglycan fragments.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SagA secretion and NlpC/p60-endopeptidase activity was required for enhancing probiotic bacteria activity against Clostridium difficile pathogenesis in vivo.
source: SagA secretion and NlpC/p60-endopeptidase activity was required for enhancing probiotic bacteria activity against Clostridium difficile pathogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection experiments with SagA mutants.

claim: The peptidoglycan composition and hydrolase activity of specific microbiota species can activate host immune pathways and enhance tolerance to pathogens.
source: Our results demonstrate that the peptidoglycan composition and hydrolase activity of specific microbiota species can activate host immune pathways and enhance tolerance to pathogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Polysaccharide A (PSA) from Bacteroides fragilis activates Toll-like receptor two on FOXP3+ regulatory T cells.
source: For example, polysaccharide A (PSA) from Bacteroides fragilis has been reported to activate Toll-like receptor two on FOXP3+ regulatory T cells, promote immunologic tolerance and enhance colonization of commensal bacteria (Round et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Round et al., 2011.

claim: Butyrate production by Clostridial strains can attenuate inflammation by inducing peripheral regulatory T cells.
source: Alternatively, butyrate production by Clostridial strains (clusters XIVa and IV) can attenuate inflammation by inducing peripheral regulatory T cells (Arpaia et al., 2013; Furusawa et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013) and suppress reactive metabolites to prevent the expansion of enteric pathogens (Byndloss et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arpaia et al., 2013; Furusawa et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013.

claim: Clostridium scindens can generate secondary bile acids that mediate colonization resistance toward Clostridium difficile.
source: In addition, commensal bacteria such as Clostridium scindens can generate secondary bile acids that mediate colonization resistance toward pathogens such as Clostridium difficile (Buffie et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Buffie et al., 2015.

claim: E. faecium is a ubiquitous bacterium that has been recovered from the microbiota of many animals as well as humans.
source: E. faecium is a ubiquitous bacterium that has been recovered from the microbiota of many animals as well as humans (Van Tyne and Gilmore, 2014) and can even colonize the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) (Garsin et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Van Tyne and Gilmore, 2014 and Garsin et al., 2001.

claim: E. faecium can colonize C. elegans.
source: E. faecium is a ubiquitous bacterium that has been recovered from the microbiota of many animals as well as humans (Van Tyne and Gilmore, 2014) and can even colonize the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) (Garsin et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garsin et al., 2001.

claim: Pathogenic strains of E. faecium and E. faecalis are notable due to their acquisition of drug-resistance and nosocomial infections.
source: While pathogenic strains of E. faecium and E. faecalis are notable due to their acquisition of drug-resistance and nosocomial infections (Arias and Murray, 2012), commensal strains of E. faecium have been reported to protect animals from enteric pathogens and potentially improve host metabolism (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arias and Murray, 2012.

claim: Commensal strains of E. faecium have been reported to protect animals from enteric pathogens and potentially improve host metabolism.
source: While pathogenic strains of E. faecium and E. faecalis are notable due to their acquisition of drug-resistance and nosocomial infections (Arias and Murray, 2012), commensal strains of E. faecium have been reported to protect animals from enteric pathogens and potentially improve host metabolism (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2016.

claim: Diverse strains of E. faecium could protect worms against enteric pathogens.
source: To dissect the protective mechanisms of E. faecium, we utilized C. elegans as an animal model and discovered that diverse strains of E. faecium could protect worms against enteric pathogens (Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium and its growth media effectively prevented Salmonella Typhimurium-induced pathogenesis in C. elegans.
source: E. faecium and its growth media effectively prevented Salmonella Typhimurium-induced pathogenesis in C. elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior experimental data.

claim: The protective activity of E. faecium growth media was protease sensitive.
source: The protective activity of E. faecium growth media was protease sensitive, which led to the proteomic analysis of the supernatant and discovery of secreted antigen A (SagA) as one of the most abundant E. faecium secreted proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing protease sensitivity.

claim: SagA is one of the most abundant E. faecium secreted proteins.
source: The protective activity of E. faecium growth media was protease sensitive, which led to the proteomic analysis of the supernatant and discovery of secreted antigen A (SagA) as one of the most abundant E. faecium secreted proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic analysis data.

claim: Administration of recombinant SagA to C. elegans was sufficient to attenuate S. Typhimurium pathogenesis.
source: Remarkably, administration of recombinant SagA to C. elegans was sufficient to attenuate S. Typhimurium pathogenesis (Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: Chromosomal insertion of sagA into E. faecalis enabled the expression and secretion of SagA, which conferred protective activity against S. Typhimurium pathogenesis in C. elegans.
source: In addition, chromosomal insertion of sagA into non-protective E. faecalis (E. faecalis-sagA) enabled the expression and secretion of SagA, which also conferred protective activity against S. Typhimurium pathogenesis in C. elegans (Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium and SagA did not affect S. Typhimurium colonization or replication in vivo.
source: E. faecium and SagA did not affect S. Typhimurium colonization or replication in vivo, but rather required tol-1 signaling in C. elegans, suggesting the activation of host innate immunity was the key mechanism for enhanced tolerance against enteric pathogens (Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium and SagA required tol-1 signaling in C. elegans for protective activity.
source: E. faecium and SagA did not affect S. Typhimurium colonization or replication in vivo, but rather required tol-1 signaling in C. elegans, suggesting the activation of host innate immunity was the key mechanism for enhanced tolerance against enteric pathogens (Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium colonization improved intestinal barrier morphology, permeability, gene expression (Muc2, cryptdin2 and RegIIIγ) and prevented S. Typhimurium pathogenesis in mice.
source: In these studies, E. faecium colonization, but not E. faecalis, improved intestinal barrier morphology, permeability, gene expression (Muc2, cryptdin2 and RegIIIγ) and prevented S. Typhimurium pathogenesis (Pedicord et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecalis colonization did not improve intestinal barrier morphology, permeability, gene expression or prevent S. Typhimurium pathogenesis in mice.
source: In these studies, E. faecium colonization, but not E. faecalis, improved intestinal barrier morphology, permeability, gene expression (Muc2, cryptdin2 and RegIIIγ) and prevented S. Typhimurium pathogenesis (Pedicord et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium required innate immune signaling factors such as MyD88 and NOD2 as well as RegIIIγ.
source: E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium did not involve adaptive immunity mechanisms, but required innate immune signaling factors such as MyD88 (Toll-like receptor adaptor) and NOD2 as well as RegIIIγ, a key effector of intestinal barrier function (Pedicord et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium did not involve adaptive immunity mechanisms.
source: E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium did not involve adaptive immunity mechanisms, but required innate immune signaling factors such as MyD88 (Toll-like receptor adaptor) and NOD2 as well as RegIIIγ, a key effector of intestinal barrier function (Pedicord et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecalis-sagA increased the expression of intestinal epithelial barrier function genes (Muc2, cryptdin2 and RegIIIγ) and enhanced bacterial segregation from intestinal epithelial cells in vivo similar to E. faecium.
source: E. faecalis-sagA also increased the expression of intestinal epithelial barrier function genes (Muc2, cryptdin2 and RegIIIγ) and enhanced bacterial segregation from intestinal epithelial cells in vivo similar to E. faecium.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior experimental data.

claim: SagA can be expressed in probiotic bacteria such as Lactobacillus plantarum and enhanced its protective activity against S. Typhimurium as well as C. difficile.
source: Moreover, SagA can be expressed in probiotic bacteria such as Lactobacillus plantarum and enhanced its protective activity against S. Typhimurium as well as C. difficile (Pedicord et al., 2016; Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pedicord et al., 2016; Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium was abrogated in Nod2-/- mice in vivo.
source: Since E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium was abrogated in Nod2-/- mice in vivo and SagA contains predicted peptidoglycan hydrolase (Pedicord et al., 2016), we focused on whether E. faecium and SagA exhibit unique peptidoglycan composition and activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016.

claim: SagA contains predicted peptidoglycan hydrolase.
source: Since E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium was abrogated in Nod2-/- mice in vivo and SagA contains predicted peptidoglycan hydrolase (Pedicord et al., 2016), we focused on whether E. faecium and SagA exhibit unique peptidoglycan composition and activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016 and bioinformatic prediction.

claim: sagA was shown to be essential for E. faecium growth.
source: As sagA was shown to be essential for E. faecium growth (Teng et al., 2003), we focused on the characterization of E. faecium (Com15), E. faecalis (OG1RF), and E. faecalis-sagA (Rangan et al., 2016), in which the sagA gene was chromosomally inserted downstream of mreD and expressed under the endogenous sagA promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Teng et al., 2003.

claim: There were comparable levels of SagA expression in the cell pellets and secretion in the supernatants of E. faecium and E. faecalis-sagA.
source: To directly compare SagA protein expression levels in these strains, we generated polyclonal sera against full length recombinant SagA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and confirmed that there were comparable levels of SagA expression in the cell pellets and secretion in the supernatants of E. faecium and E. faecalis-sagA, which was absent in E. faecalis (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: SagA was absent in E. faecalis.
source: To directly compare SagA protein expression levels in these strains, we generated polyclonal sera against full length recombinant SagA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and confirmed that there were comparable levels of SagA expression in the cell pellets and secretion in the supernatants of E. faecium and E. faecalis-sagA, which was absent in E. faecalis (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: E. faecium divided most rapidly and reached optical density values of up to OD600nm = 2.5 after 4 hr.
source: Analysis of the bacterial growth rates showed that E. faecium divided most rapidly and reached optical density values of up to OD600nm = 2.5 after 4 hr (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: E. faecalis-sagA exhibited a decreased growth rate compared to E. faecalis after 3 hr, resulting in slower exponential growth.
source: However, E. faecalis-sagA exhibited a decreased growth rate compared to E. faecalis after 3 hr, resulting in slower exponential growth (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: E. faecium exhibited unique cell wall morphology compared to E. faecalis.
source: Analysis of these bacterial strains by transmission electron microscopy showed that E. faecium exhibited unique cell wall morphology compared to E. faecalis (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1c.

claim: E. faecalis-sagA exhibited a significant increase in bacterial cell width as well as the presence of minor deformations to the integrity of the cell wall structure.
source: Interestingly, E. faecalis-sagA exhibited a significant increase in bacterial cell width as well as the presence of minor deformations to the integrity of the cell wall structure (Figure 1c,d), suggesting SagA expression may regulate cell wall composition and integrity in Enterococcus.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 1c,d.

claim: SagA expression may regulate cell wall composition and integrity in Enterococcus.
source: Interestingly, E. faecalis-sagA exhibited a significant increase in bacterial cell width as well as the presence of minor deformations to the integrity of the cell wall structure (Figure 1c,d), suggesting SagA expression may regulate cell wall composition and integrity in Enterococcus.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on observed morphological changes in E. faecalis-sagA.

claim: E. faecium generally contains non crosslinked muropeptides, including GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-isoGln (GlcNAc-MDP) compared to E. faecalis.
source: The major monomeric and crosslinked muropeptides we isolated from E. faecium and E. faecalis were similar to previous studies (Billot-Klein et al., 1996; Emirian et al., 2009; Patti et al., 2008), which showed that E. faecium generally contains non crosslinked muropeptides, including GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-isoGln (GlcNAc-MDP) compared to E. faecalis (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 2a and citations to previous studies.

claim: The analysis of peptidoglycan from E. faecalis-sagA revealed a decrease in muropeptide fragments (peak 2, 7, 9, 13, and 17) compared with E. faecalis.
source: Interestingly, the analysis of peptidoglycan from E. faecalis-sagA revealed a decrease in muropeptide fragments (peak 2, 7, 9, 13, and 17) compared with E. faecalis (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b and Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 2a and supplementary figures.

claim: Whole genome sequencing confirmed the insertion of sagA downstream of mreD in E. faecalis-sagA.
source: To evaluate whether these changes in bacterial growth, cell morphology and peptidoglycan composition were associated with SagA expression and not other mutations generated during chromosomal sagA insertion, we performed whole genome sequencing on both E. faecalis and E. faecalis-sagA. This analysis confirmed the insertion of sagA downstream of mreD, as originally designed, and also revealed a total of 39 genes with synonymous and non-synonymous mutations ranging from 25 to 100 percent coverage (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Whole genome sequencing revealed a total of 39 genes with synonymous and non-synonymous mutations in E. faecalis-sagA.
source: This analysis confirmed the insertion of sagA downstream of mreD, as originally designed, and also revealed a total of 39 genes with synonymous and non-synonymous mutations ranging from 25 to 100 percent coverage (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: None of the non-synonymous mutations greater than 50 percent coverage in E. faecalis-sagA were in genes directly associated with bacterial cell wall synthesis or remodeling.
source: However, none of the non-synonymous mutations greater than 50 percent coverage were in genes directly associated with bacterial cell wall synthesis or remodeling, suggesting SagA expression affected growth, morphology and peptidoglycan composition of E. faecalis-sagA.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data analysis.

claim: E. faecium with a multiplicity of infection (MOI = 1) activated NOD2, but not NOD1.
source: Compared to synthetic ligands iE-DAP and MDP, E. faecium with a multiplicity of infection (MOI = 1) activated NOD2, but not NOD1 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by NOD1/NOD2 activation assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: E. faecalis and E. faecalis-sagA required 10^3-fold more bacteria (MOI = 10^3) to activate NOD2, but not NOD1.
source: In contrast, E. faecalis and E. faecalis-sagA required 103-fold more bacteria (MOI = 103) to activate NOD2, but not NOD1 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by NOD1/NOD2 activation assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The selective activation of NOD2 is consistent with its agonist specificity for Lys-type muropeptides, which were found in Enterococci peptidoglycan.
source: The selective activation of NOD2 is consistent with its agonist specificity for Lys-type muropeptides, which were found in Enterococci peptidoglycan (Billot-Klein et al., 1996; Emirian et al., 2009; Patti et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by known NOD2 specificity and citations to previous studies.

claim: More E. faecium was recovered from gentamicin protection assays compared to E. faecalis and E. faecalis-sagA.
source: The differences in NOD2 activation by E. faecium compared to E. faecalis and E. faecalis-sagA may be due to enhanced bacterial adhesion and/or internalization since more E. faecium was recovered from gentamicin protection assays (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: SagA encodes an N-terminal signal sequence, predicted coiled-coil domain, Ser/Thr-rich linker region and C-terminal NlpC/p60-family peptidase domain.
source: SagA encodes an N-terminal signal sequence, predicted coiled-coil domain, Ser/Thr-rich linker region and C-terminal NlpC/p60-family peptidase domain (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: SagA is unique to E. faecium, with no clear homologues with greater than 25% protein sequence identity in most sequenced strains of E. faecalis.
source: Bioinformatic analysis suggested that SagA is unique to E. faecium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), with no clear homologues with greater than 25% protein sequence identity in most sequenced strains of E. faecalis (Neumann et al., 2019; Palmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: The SagA from E. faecium Com15 shares significant protein sequence similarity to other NlpC/p60 orthologs in other E. faecium strains.
source: Nonetheless, the SagA from E. faecium Com15 does share significant protein sequence similarity to other NlpC/p60 orthologs in other E. faecium strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The NlpC/p60-family peptidase domain and conserved active site residues were required for SagA-mediated protection in C. elegans.
source: Indeed, we demonstrated that the NlpC/p60-family peptidase domain and conserved active site residues were required for SagA-mediated protection in C. elegans (Rangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain contained the typical features of the cysteine peptidase fold.
source: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain contained the typical features of the cysteine peptidase fold (Anantharaman and Aravind, 2003), a central six-stranded, antiparallel β-sheet flanked by three surrounding α-helices (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 3c and citation.

claim: The overall dimensions of the SagA-NlpC/p60 structure were about 32.5 × 30×23 Å.
source: The overall dimensions of the structure were about 32.5 × 30×23 Å (Figure 3d) and shared significant structural homology to other NlpC/p60 hydrolase domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 structure shared significant structural homology to other NlpC/p60 hydrolase domains.
source: The overall dimensions of the structure were about 32.5 × 30×23 Å (Figure 3d) and shared significant structural homology to other NlpC/p60 hydrolase domains. The root-mean-square deviations between superimposed Cα atoms was a range of 1.6 ~ 2.0 Å when comparing with NlpC/p60 hydrolase domains of other structures (Supplementary file 6 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The conserved catalytic triad (C443, H494 and H506) of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain was located in a putative substrate-binding groove between the subdomains in the α2 and β3–β4.
source: The conserved catalytic triad (C443, H494 and H506) of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain was located in a putative substrate-binding groove between the subdomains in the α2 and β3–β4 (Figure 3c,d), where electron density for these key amino acid residues were well observed (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 3c,d,e.

claim: The putative substrate-binding groove of SagA-NlpC/p60 was mostly composed of negatively charged amino acid residues.
source: An electrostatic potential analysis of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain showed that the putative substrate-binding groove was mostly composed of negatively charged amino acid residues (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrostatic potential analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The residues with the highest percentage of conservation in SagA-NlpC/p60 were in the active site in the putative substrate binding pocket.
source: Homology-based structural search using ConSurf server suggested that the residues with the highest percentage of conservation were in the active site in the putative substrate binding pocket.
evidence: This claim is supported by conservation analysis using ConSurf server.

claim: Recombinant SagA constructs did not cleave purified intact E. faecium peptidoglycan.
source: These recombinant SagA constructs did not cleave purified intact E. faecium peptidoglycan, but incubation of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain with mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan yielded small muropeptides by in-gel fluorescence profiling (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: Incubation of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain with mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan yielded small muropeptides.
source: These recombinant SagA constructs did not cleave purified intact E. faecium peptidoglycan, but incubation of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain with mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan yielded small muropeptides by in-gel fluorescence profiling (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain only cleaved mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan from E. faecium and E. faecalis, but not E. coli.
source: Intriguingly, the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain only cleaved mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan from E. faecium and E. faecalis, but not E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d), which suggested that it may be specific for L-Lys-type peptidoglycan found in Enterococcus versus mDAP-type in E. coli.
evidence: This claim is supported by in-gel fluorescence profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3d.

claim: SagA-NlpC/p60 may be specific for L-Lys-type peptidoglycan found in Enterococcus versus mDAP-type in E. coli.
source: Intriguingly, the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain only cleaved mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan from E. faecium and E. faecalis, but not E. coli (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d), which suggested that it may be specific for L-Lys-type peptidoglycan found in Enterococcus versus mDAP-type in E. coli.
evidence: This claim is inferred from substrate specificity data.

claim: LC-MS analysis of the full-length SagA and SagA-NlpC/p60 reaction products revealed the generation of several new peptidoglycan fragments as enzymatic products.
source: LC-MS analysis of the full-length SagA and SagA-NlpC/p60 reaction products revealed the generation of several new peptidoglycan fragments as enzymatic products such as tripeptide (peak a), GlcNAc-MDP (peak b), GlcNAc-MurNAc-tri-di (peak c), GlcNAc-MurNAc-tetra-tri (peak d) and larger fragments (peak e) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e and Supplementary file 4), which were absent when the full-length SagA-C443A and the SagA-NlpC/p60-C443A active site mutants were added.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3e.

claim: Full-length SagA expressed and purified from E. coli was less active with mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan than truncated SagA-NlpC/p60 domain.
source: Full-length SagA expressed and purified from E. coli at similar protein concentrations was less active with mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan than truncated SagA-NlpC/p60 domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e), suggesting the N-terminus may inhibit or modulate the activity of NlpC/p60 domain, akin to the coiled-coil domain of PcsB from Streptococcus pneumonia (Bartual et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3e.

claim: The N-terminus of SagA may inhibit or modulate the activity of NlpC/p60 domain.
source: Full-length SagA expressed and purified from E. coli at similar protein concentrations was less active with mutanolysin-digested peptidoglycan than truncated SagA-NlpC/p60 domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e), suggesting the N-terminus may inhibit or modulate the activity of NlpC/p60 domain, akin to the coiled-coil domain of PcsB from Streptococcus pneumonia (Bartual et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative based on activity differences and comparison to PcsB.

claim: Gel-filtration analysis revealed that SagA-NlpC/p60 is monomeric.
source: Gel-filtration analysis revealed that SagA-NlpC/p60 is monomeric (Figure 3b) and amenable to crystallization (Supplementary Results).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel-filtration data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The structure of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain was solved to 2.4 Å resolution by using X-ray crystallography.
source: The structure of the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain was solved to 2.4 Å resolution by using X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: Manual inspection of the top-posed GlcNAc-MurNAc-tetrapeptide docked into the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain showed the predicted active site cysteine (C443) and histidine residues (H494 and H506) were well positioned near the potential site of peptide bond cleavage.
source: Manual inspection of the top-posed GlcNAc-MurNAc-tetrapeptide docked into the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain showed the predicted active site cysteine (C443) and histidine residues (H494 and H506) were well positioned near the potential site of peptide bond cleavage (Figure 4c, pose one from Supplementary file 7) and suggested peptidoglycan fragments may extend across the putative substrate-binding groove to interact with electropositive amino acid residues on the potential glycan and peptide binding sites at the surface (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by docking studies shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 ligand-docked models suggested that two tryptophans (W433 and W462) may serve as clamps for binding potential peptidoglycan substrates.
source: Interestingly, the SagA-NlpC/p60 ligand-docked models also suggested that two tryptophans (W433 and W462) may serve as clamps for binding potential peptidoglycan substrates (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This claim is inferred from docking studies shown in Figure 4b,c.

claim: Single and double Ala mutants of W433 and W462 significantly abrogated hydrolytic activity of SagA-NlpC/p60 domain.
source: Indeed, single and double Ala mutants of W433 and W462 significantly abrogated hydrolytic activity of SagA-NlpC/p60 domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and activity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: C443, W433 and W462 are crucial for the SagA-NlpC/p60 peptidoglycan hydrolase activity.
source: These results demonstrate C443, W433 and W462 are crucial for the SagA-NlpC/p60 peptidoglycan hydrolase activity and encompass the enzyme active site as well as putative substrate-binding groove.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and activity assay data.

claim: Disaccharide-tripeptide, disaccharide-tetrapeptide and disaccharide-pentapeptide were not cleaved or only showed modest production of GlcNAc-MDP by SagA-NlpC/p60.
source: Disaccharide-tripeptide, disaccharide-tetrapeptide and disaccharide-pentapeptide were not cleaved or only showed modest production of GlcNAc-MDP (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a,b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a,b,c.

claim: Incubation of SagA-NlpC/p60 with disaccharide-tripeptide crosslinked to disaccharide-tetrapeptide readily generated GlcNAc-MDP and the corresponding GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-isoGln-L-Lys-crosslinked-D-Ala-L-Lys heptapeptide product (GlcNAc-M7P).
source: However, incubation of SagA-NlpC/p60 with disaccharide-tripeptide crosslinked to disaccharide-tetrapeptide readily generated GlcNAc-MDP and the corresponding GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-isoGln-L-Lys-crosslinked-D-Ala-L-Lys heptapeptide product (GlcNAc-M7P) (Figure 4d) and Figure 4—figure supplement 3d) with a specific activity of approximately 67 ± 7 nmol/min/mg at 37°C (Figure 4e), which did not occur with the NlpC/p60-C443A mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 3d.

claim: SagA-NlpC/p60 has a specific activity of approximately 67 ± 7 nmol/min/mg at 37°C with disaccharide-tripeptide crosslinked to disaccharide-tetrapeptide.
source: However, incubation of SagA-NlpC/p60 with disaccharide-tripeptide crosslinked to disaccharide-tetrapeptide readily generated GlcNAc-MDP and the corresponding GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-isoGln-L-Lys-crosslinked-D-Ala-L-Lys heptapeptide product (GlcNAc-M7P) (Figure 4d) and Figure 4—figure supplement 3d) with a specific activity of approximately 67 ± 7 nmol/min/mg at 37°C (Figure 4e), which did not occur with the NlpC/p60-C443A mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by specific activity measurement data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: SagA-NlpC/p60 encodes cysteine endopeptidase activity that prefers crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments and cleaves the peptide bond between D-iGln and L-Lys.
source: These results demonstrated that SagA-NlpC/p60 encodes cysteine endopeptidase activity that prefers crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments and cleaves the peptide bond between D-iGln and L-Lys (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity and product analysis data.

claim: SagA-generated and synthetic GlcNAc-MDP activated NOD2 in a dose-dependent manner comparable to commercial MDP standard.
source: Using NOD1 and NOD2 HEK-Blue cells that exhibited better dose-response to ligands, we found that SagA-generated and synthetic GlcNAc-MDP activated NOD2 in a dose-dependent manner comparable to commercial MDP standard (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by NOD2 activation assay data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: SagA-NlpC/p60-generated muropeptides, GlcNAc-MDP most effectively activated NOD2, and GlcNAc-M7P less effectively and both ligands were more active than the crosslinked peptidoglycan fragment.
source: SagA-NlpC/p60-generated muropeptides, GlcNAc-MDP most effectively activated NOD2, and GlcNAc-M7P less effectively and both ligands were more active than the crosslinked peptidoglycan fragment (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by NOD2 activation assay data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Non-crosslinked muropeptides more effectively activate NOD2 in mammalian cells.
source: Importantly, these results indicated non-crosslinked muropeptides more effectively activate NOD2 in mammalian cells and provides a biochemical mechanism by which E. faecium and secreted SagA may enhance host immunity toward enteric pathogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by NOD2 activation assay data.

claim: Chromosomal insertion of a SagA active site mutant into E. faecalis yielded low or undetectable levels of protein expression in cell lysate or supernatant.
source: While chromosomal insertion of sagA into E. faecalis was functional (Rangan et al., 2016), insertion of a SagA active site mutant yielded low or undetectable levels of protein expression in cell lysate or supernatant (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Plasmid-based expression of SagA-His6 variants in L. plantarum yielded comparable levels of wild-type SagA, signal sequence mutant (ΔSS) as well as active site mutant (C443A) in cell lysates.
source: However, plasmid-based expression of SagA-His6 variants in L. plantarum yielded comparable levels of wild-type SagA, signal sequence mutant (ΔSS) as well as active site mutant (C443A) in cell lysates, with reduced levels of ΔSS mutant in the supernatant (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Heterologous expression of SagA variants did not significantly alter the L. plantarum peptidoglycan composition (amidated mDAP-type).
source: Heterologous expression of these SagA variants did not significantly alter the L. plantarum peptidoglycan composition (amidated mDAP-type) (Goffin et al., 2005) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation.

claim: Colonization of antibiotic-treated mice with L. plantarum expressing wild-type SagA protected mice from C. difficile pathogenesis.
source: However, colonization of antibiotic (Abx)-treated mice with these L. plantarum strains showed that wild-type SagA protected mice from C. difficile pathogenesis, while the SagA signal sequence (ΔSS) as well as active site (C443A) mutant were not protective and comparable to L. plantarum-vector and PBS controls (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection experiment data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The SagA signal sequence (ΔSS) as well as active site (C443A) mutant were not protective against C. difficile pathogenesis in mice.
source: However, colonization of antibiotic (Abx)-treated mice with these L. plantarum strains showed that wild-type SagA protected mice from C. difficile pathogenesis, while the SagA signal sequence (ΔSS) as well as active site (C443A) mutant were not protective and comparable to L. plantarum-vector and PBS controls (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo infection experiment data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: E. faecium protection against S. Typhimurium was abrogated in Nod2-/- mice in vivo.
source: Indeed, our previous studies showed that NOD2 was required for E. faecium-mediated protection against enteric pathogen infection (Pedicord et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pedicord et al., 2016.

claim: E. faecium peptidoglycan contains smaller non-crosslinked muropeptides compared to non-protective strains of E. faecalis.
source: Here, we demonstrated that E. faecium peptidoglycan contains smaller non-crosslinked muropeptides compared to non-protective strains of E. faecalis, which more effectively activated the intracellular peptidoglycan pattern recognition receptor NOD2.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptidoglycan analysis and NOD2 activation data.

claim: E. faecium peptidoglycan more effectively activated the intracellular peptidoglycan pattern recognition receptor NOD2 compared to E. faecalis.
source: Here, we demonstrated that E. faecium peptidoglycan contains smaller non-crosslinked muropeptides compared to non-protective strains of E. faecalis, which more effectively activated the intracellular peptidoglycan pattern recognition receptor NOD2.
evidence: This claim is supported by NOD2 activation assay data.

claim: The X-ray structure of the E. faecium SagA-NlpC/p60 catalytic domain was determined.
source: In addition, we determined the X-ray structure of the E. faecium SagA-NlpC/p60 catalytic domain and showed that it encodes L-Lys-type endopeptidase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain encodes L-Lys-type endopeptidase activity.
source: In addition, we determined the X-ray structure of the E. faecium SagA-NlpC/p60 catalytic domain and showed that it encodes L-Lys-type endopeptidase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity data.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain selectively cleaved purified crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments into smaller muropeptides, which were more active towards NOD2 in mammalian cells.
source: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain selectively cleaved purified crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments into smaller muropeptides, which were more active towards NOD2 in mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity and NOD2 activation data.

claim: E. faecium may be intrinsically more capable of interacting with mammalian cells and/or directly activate NOD2 even though both Enterococci species have Lys-type peptidoglycan.
source: The results suggested E. faecium may be intrinsically more capable of interacting with mammalian cells and/or directly activate NOD2 even though both Enterococci species have Lys-type peptidoglycan.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparative NOD2 activation data.

claim: SagA expression still enhances the protective activity of E. faecalis and L. plantarum against enteric pathogens in vivo.
source: Nonetheless, SagA expression still enhances the protective activity of E. faecalis and L. plantarum against enteric pathogens in vivo (Pedicord et al., 2016; Rangan et al., 2016), suggesting secreted SagA may also prime or activate immune pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pedicord et al., 2016; Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: Secreted SagA may prime or activate immune pathways.
source: Nonetheless, SagA expression still enhances the protective activity of E. faecalis and L. plantarum against enteric pathogens in vivo (Pedicord et al., 2016; Rangan et al., 2016), suggesting secreted SagA may also prime or activate immune pathways.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on in vivo protective activity.

claim: Full-length SagA purified from E. coli was active.
source: Although full-length SagA purified from E. coli was active, we focused on the C-terminal NlpC/p60 hydrolase domain since it was significantly more active in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity data.

claim: The C-terminal NlpC/p60 hydrolase domain was significantly more active in vitro than full-length SagA.
source: Although full-length SagA purified from E. coli was active, we focused on the C-terminal NlpC/p60 hydrolase domain since it was significantly more active in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity data.

claim: The SagA-NlpC/p60 domain was similar to other bacterial hydrolases and shared similar active site residues.
source: X-ray crystallography showed that the SagA-NlpC/p60 domain was indeed similar to other bacterial hydrolases and shared similar active site residues (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Analysis of SagA-NlpC/p60 domain with purified peptidoglycan fragments demonstrated that it showed endopeptidase activity and preferentially cleaved L-Lys-type crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments.
source: Analysis of SagA-NlpC/p60 domain with purified peptidoglycan fragments demonstrated that it showed endopeptidase activity and preferentially cleaved L-Lys-type crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments (Figure 4), which required the conserved active site Cys443.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The endopeptidase activity of SagA-NlpC/p60 required the conserved active site Cys443.
source: Analysis of SagA-NlpC/p60 domain with purified peptidoglycan fragments demonstrated that it showed endopeptidase activity and preferentially cleaved L-Lys-type crosslinked peptidoglycan fragments (Figure 4), which required the conserved active site Cys443.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and enzymatic activity data.

claim: W433 and W462 were essential for the endopeptidase activity in vitro and may be involved in stabilization of the peptidoglycan substrate binding.
source: In addition, W433 and W462 were also essential for the endopeptidase activity in vitro and may be involved in stabilization of the peptidoglycan substrate binding based on our SagA-NlpC/p60 structure and docking studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis, enzymatic activity, and docking data.

claim: Tryptophan residues or other hydrophobic aromatic amino acids are highly conserved amongst other SagA orthologs in Enterococci as well as other hydrolases in other bacteria.
source: These tryptophan residues or other hydrophobic aromatic amino acids are highly conserved amongst other SagA orthologs in Enterococci as well as other hydrolases in other bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The molecular basis for Lys- or DAP-type peptidoglycan specificity is still unclear from existing NlpC/p60 hydrolases structures.
source: Beyond these highly conserved amino acid residues in the SagA-NlpC/p60 active site, the molecular basis for Lys- or DAP-type peptidoglycan specificity is still unclear from ours and other existing NlpC/p60 hydrolases structures (Xu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2014b; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: SagA-NlpC/p60 generated non-crosslinked muropeptides such as GlcNAc-MDP, which were also found in E. faecium peptidoglycan and activated NOD2 in mammalian cells more effectively than larger and crosslinked muropeptides.
source: Notably, these studies demonstrated that SagA-NlpC/p60 generated non-crosslinked muropeptides such as GlcNAc-MDP, which were also found in E. faecium peptidoglycan and activated NOD2 in mammalian cells more effectively than larger and crosslinked muropeptides (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity and NOD2 activation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: E. faecium and its secreted peptidoglycan hydrolase SagA generates small muropeptides that activate NOD2, which triggers downstream signaling pathways to enhance intestinal barrier function and host immunity.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that E. faecium and its secreted peptidoglycan hydrolase SagA generates small muropeptides that activate NOD2, which triggers downstream signaling pathways to enhance intestinal barrier function and host immunity (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the collective experimental data and shown in Figure 6.

claim: MDP were not active in C. elegans, which does not have a clear NOD2 ortholog.
source: Although MDP were not active in C. elegans, which does not have a clear NOD2 ortholog, MurNAc and MurNAc-L-Ala were sufficient to attenuate bacterial pathogenesis and required the Tol-1 signaling (Rangan et al., 2016), suggesting the recognition of small bacteria-specific glycans may also be conserved in nematodes but utilize different receptors akin to insects (Dziarski and Gupta, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: MurNAc and MurNAc-L-Ala were sufficient to attenuate bacterial pathogenesis in C. elegans and required the Tol-1 signaling.
source: Although MDP were not active in C. elegans, which does not have a clear NOD2 ortholog, MurNAc and MurNAc-L-Ala were sufficient to attenuate bacterial pathogenesis and required the Tol-1 signaling (Rangan et al., 2016), suggesting the recognition of small bacteria-specific glycans may also be conserved in nematodes but utilize different receptors akin to insects (Dziarski and Gupta, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rangan et al., 2016.

claim: The recognition of small bacteria-specific glycans may be conserved in nematodes but utilize different receptors akin to insects.
source: Although MDP were not active in C. elegans, which does not have a clear NOD2 ortholog, MurNAc and MurNAc-L-Ala were sufficient to attenuate bacterial pathogenesis and required the Tol-1 signaling (Rangan et al., 2016), suggesting the recognition of small bacteria-specific glycans may also be conserved in nematodes but utilize different receptors akin to insects (Dziarski and Gupta, 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculative based on C. elegans data and comparison to insects.

claim: Smaller muropeptide fragments have been reported to enhance NOD2 activation ex vivo.
source: In mammals, smaller muropeptide fragments have been reported to enhance NOD2 activation ex vivo (Dagil et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2011; Fujimoto et al., 2009; Girardin et al., 2003a; Wang et al., 2013) and function as more effective adjuvants for vaccination (Hancock et al., 2012; Ogawa et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2013) or enhance monocyte activity in vivo (Coulombe et al., 2012; Namba et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Smaller muropeptide fragments function as more effective adjuvants for vaccination.
source: In mammals, smaller muropeptide fragments have been reported to enhance NOD2 activation ex vivo (Dagil et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2011; Fujimoto et al., 2009; Girardin et al., 2003a; Wang et al., 2013) and function as more effective adjuvants for vaccination (Hancock et al., 2012; Ogawa et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2013) or enhance monocyte activity in vivo (Coulombe et al., 2012; Namba et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hancock et al., 2012; Ogawa et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2013.

claim: Smaller muropeptide fragments enhance monocyte activity in vivo.
source: In mammals, smaller muropeptide fragments have been reported to enhance NOD2 activation ex vivo (Dagil et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2011; Fujimoto et al., 2009; Girardin et al., 2003a; Wang et al., 2013) and function as more effective adjuvants for vaccination (Hancock et al., 2012; Ogawa et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2013) or enhance monocyte activity in vivo (Coulombe et al., 2012; Namba et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coulombe et al., 2012; Namba et al., 1996.

claim: NOD2 is important for modulating immune signaling in many areas of host physiology and disease.
source: Since NOD2 is important for modulating immune signaling in many areas of host physiology and disease (Caruso et al., 2014; Keestra-Gounder and Tsolis, 2017; Philpott et al., 2014), further analysis of Enterococci and SagA orthologs will be important for understanding specific microbiota-host interactions and may afford new opportunities for therapeutic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caruso et al., 2014; Keestra-Gounder and Tsolis, 2017; Philpott et al., 2014.
